product-launch.name: Product Launch
product-launch.summary: Persuasive launch arc: open with brand, hook with a promise, set the conflict, raise the stakes, reveal the product, raise stakes again, sell, and call to action. Tuned for keynote-style launches and major announcement decks.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Open with the company brand and a confident visual. Set the tone — this is a moment, not a meeting. One slide that signals the audience is somewhere worth being.

beats.name: Promise
beats.description: Hook the audience with the promise of the talk. Tell them, in one sentence, what they're about to see and why it matters to them. Specific promises buy patient audiences.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Set the stage with the world the product enters. The customer reality, the market state, the unmet expectation. Context turns the launch from a product release into a moment in a larger story.

beats.name: Conflict
beats.description: Introduce the villain — the problem, friction, or status quo the product opposes. Make the conflict concrete enough that the audience can name a moment they've felt it themselves.

beats.name: Stakes
beats.description: Emphasize what's at risk if the conflict isn't resolved. Quantify, personalize, dramatize. Stakes are what convert a curious audience into an invested one.

beats.name: Reveal
beats.description: Showcase the product. One striking visual, one defining capability, one sentence that captures what's new. Earn the applause line; don't bury it under a bullet list.

beats.name: Raise the Stakes
beats.description: Highlight where the alternatives fall short and what they cost the customer. Re-energize the room midway by sharpening the contrast with the reveal.

beats.name: Reinforce the Need
beats.description: Reinforce why change is non-negotiable now. A second beat of stakes, framed differently — perhaps a customer voice or a future cost. Cement the reason to act.

beats.name: Sell
beats.description: Make the audience want the product. Lead with the outcome it produces in their lives. Pricing, packaging, availability go here, but only after the desire is built.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Close with the single action you want from the audience. Pre-order, sign up, attend, share. Make it simple, specific, and immediate.

marketing.name: Marketing
marketing.summary: Marketing professionals analyzing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategies.
marketing.description: Marketing professionals reviewing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategy. Make the funnel visible, highlight engagement metrics, keep the brand consistent, and tell the story visually. Moderate chart density; 15-30 slides.

sales.name: Sales
sales.summary: Sales team or prospective customers focused on product benefits, competitive differentiation, and ROI justification.
sales.description: Sales teams and prospective customers weighing product benefits, competitive differentiation, and ROI. Put customer success stories first, back claims with visual proof points, state the value proposition plainly, and close on a strong call to action. Moderate chart density; 15-25 slides.

educate.name: Educate
educate.summary: Teach a concept, process, product, or domain so the audience can use it correctly.
educate.description: Use when the primary job is learning. Structure around concepts, examples, practice, and checks for understanding rather than persuasion or reporting.
educate.outcome: The audience understands the material well enough to apply it.

inspirational.name: Inspirational
inspirational.summary: Aspirational, narrative-driven voice for keynotes, founders, and rallying cries.
inspirational.description: Reach for shared belief and possibility, then ground it in something concrete. Use vivid imagery and rhythm; avoid collapsing into hype by always pairing aspiration with a real anchor.
voiceCues: Open with belief; close with action.
Use rhythm — paired phrases, repetition, deliberate beats.
Pair every aspirational claim with a concrete proof point.
Speak in present tense to make the future feel inevitable.
avoid: Stacked superlatives ('the very best, world-changing, revolutionary').
Dense data tables — push numbers into supporting slides.
samplePhrases: We're building the runtime that makes agents feel instant.
When latency disappears, what becomes possible?
The next decade of software belongs to teams who treat speed as a feature.

classic.name: Classic

cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
